clue.text: Officer involved in a pact with musicians

parts.note: a band of musicians is a group

indicators.note: involved means twisted up, so the letters of in a pact are tangled into a new order

explanation.surface: An officer gets mixed up in a deal with a band.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved' looks like 'taking part', but it signals that the letters of 'in a pact' are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A group captain is a senior commissioned rank in the Royal Air Force.

clue.text: Girl, egg shaped, one with a silly laugh

indicators.note: shaped means formed anew, so the letters of girl and egg are moulded into another order

explanation.surface: An egg-shaped girl who titters foolishly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shaped' rearranges GIRL plus EGG.
explanation.definitionFit: A giggler is someone who titters in a nervous or foolish way.

clue.text: University score almost exceeded

parts.note: OU is the Open University, a British distance-learning institution

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the number word loses its last letter

parts.note: a score is twenty

explanation.surface: A university's tally nearly went over the top.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' cuts the Y from TWENTY. OU stands for the Open University, Britain's distance-learning university.
explanation.definitionFit: To outgo something is to surpass or go beyond it, so the past form means surpassed.

clue.text: It may indirectly reflect the views of submariners

definitions.text: It may indirectly reflect the views of submariners

parts.words: It may indirectly reflect the views of submariners
parts.note: read literally: a device whose mirrors bounce the scene above the waves down to people in a submerged boat, so the views reach them indirectly

explanation.surface: Something that hints at the opinions of naval crews.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reflect the views' sounds like expressing opinions, but it means mirrors relaying a sight.
explanation.definitionFit: A periscope uses mirrors or prisms to let a submerged crew see above the surface.

clue.text: A ray appears, at right angles to the vessel

definitions.text: at right angles to the vessel

parts.note: a beam is a ray of light

explanation.surface: A shaft of light shows up across a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Abeam is a nautical term for a direction perpendicular to a ship's keel.

clue.text: Aimed to educate a journalist

parts.note: to train someone is to teach them
ED, short for editor, is the crossword journalist

explanation.surface: A plan to school a reporter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Aimed' looks like 'intended' but is the sense of pointing a gun.
explanation.definitionFit: A gun trained on a target is pointed at it, so the word means directed.

clue.text: Temporary Head of English enters, looking smart and healthy

indicators.note: enters says the leading letter goes inside the phrase

parts.note: in trim means neat and in good condition

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A stand-in head teacher of English arrives looking fit and neat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head of' gives E; 'enters' puts it inside IN TRIM.
explanation.definitionFit: An interim arrangement is provisional, holding until a permanent one is found.

clue.text: Smooth progress in prairies, having an 11

parts.note: prairies are grassy plains
11 across is a complaint, so having one is being sick

explanation.surface: Easy going across the open grasslands, despite being unwell.
explanation.walkthrough: '11' points to the answer at 11 across, a sickness; having one is AILING.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain sailing is an idiom for a straightforward, untroubled course of action.

clue.text: Irritating fellow losing his head in boat

indicators.note: the fellow's word loses its opening letter, its head

parts.note: blighter is British slang for an annoying man

explanation.surface: An annoying man is beheaded aboard a vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing his head' drops the B from BLIGHTER, a mildly rude British word for a tiresome person.
explanation.definitionFit: A lighter is a flat-bottomed barge used to ferry goods to and from ships.

clue.text: Adaptable, porter, say, rejected verbal criticism

indicators.note: rejected means sent back, so the word ale is read backwards

parts.note: porter is a dark beer, an example of ale

indicators.note: verbal means spoken, so the word for criticism is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: stick is British slang for harsh criticism, as in 'to give someone stick'

explanation.surface: A flexible person, a railway porter perhaps, brushed off spoken criticism.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejected' turns ALE into ELA; 'verbal' gives the sound of STICK, written STIC, as it is said at the end of the answer. 'porter' looks like a carrier but is the beer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something elastic stretches and bends, so it is flexible, able to fit changing needs.

clue.text: Interchange of argument familiar to fencers

explanation.surface: Debate compared with swordplay.
explanation.walkthrough: Fencers literally cut (slash) and thrust (stab); the phrase is used figuratively for lively debate.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means a lively exchange of views, and literally names sword strokes of slashing and stabbing.

clue.text: Complaint from State head

parts.note: ILL is the abbreviation for Illinois, a US state
a ness is a headland, a head of land jutting into the sea, as in Loch Ness's neighbours

explanation.surface: A grievance comes from the head of state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State head' reads as head of state; a ness is a headland, as in place names on the British coast.
explanation.definitionFit: A complaint in the medical sense is a disorder or sickness.

clue.text: Difficult term in a slender tower

indicators.note: difficult letters are awkward ones that must be wrestled into a new order

explanation.surface: A hard word turns up in a description of a thin tower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Difficult' rearranges TERM IN A.
explanation.definitionFit: A minaret is the tall thin tower of a mosque, from which the call to prayer is made.

clue.text: Southern Irishman catching river fish

indicators.note: catching means holding inside, so one piece goes into the middle of the name

parts.note: Pat, short for Patrick, is the stock Irishman of crosswords

explanation.surface: A man from the south of Ireland lands a fish from the river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'catching' puts R inside PAT, after S.
explanation.definitionFit: A sprat is a small silvery sea creature of the herring family.

clue.text: Commissioner shoots leader of militants in sultanate

indicators.note: in puts the shoots and the leading letter inside the country

parts.note: Oman on the Arabian peninsula is ruled by a sultan
buds are young shoots on a plant

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: An official guns down a rebel chief in an Arab state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shoots' looks like a verb of firing, but it is a noun for new growth on a plant; 'in' puts it and the militants' leader inside the sultanate.
explanation.definitionFit: An ombudsman is an official appointed to investigate complaints against public bodies.

clue.text: Club celebrity seen around army infantry unit

indicators.note: seen around says the club and celebrity pieces surround the army's letters

parts.note: a bat is a club used in sport
a lion is a celebrated person, as in literary lion
TA is the Territorial Army, Britain's volunteer reserve force

explanation.surface: A golf club's star player is spotted near a military unit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seen around' wraps club and celebrity round the Territorial Army, Britain's reserve force. 'army' sits beside the definition but is wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A battalion is a large body of foot soldiers, part of a regiment or brigade.

clue.text: Faulty indicator of time?

explanation.surface: A broken clock is a poor timekeeper.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is grammatical: the imperfect is a verb tense showing continuing past action, so it indicates time.
explanation.definitionFit: Faulty things have flaws; in grammar the imperfect tense marks ongoing past action.

clue.text: Naval commander holds up drink and cereal

indicators.note: holds up in a down entry means the commander's letters sit beneath the drink, supporting it

parts.note: pop is a fizzy soft drink
CO is commanding officer and RN the Royal Navy

explanation.surface: A navy captain raises a glass and eats breakfast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holds up' works because the clue runs down: CORN goes below POP.
explanation.definitionFit: Popcorn is maize kernels heated until they burst, a grain-based snack.

clue.text: Broken her shin? It's the wine!

indicators.note: broken means smashed into bits, so the letters of her shin are reassembled

explanation.surface: She hurt her leg and blames the drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broken' rearranges HER SHIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhenish is wine from the Rhine region, an old name for hock.

clue.text: Sounds like a snack served in the bay

indicators.note: sounds like says the snack's word is heard, not spelt

parts.note: a bite is a quick light meal

explanation.surface: A light meal is eaten beside the bay.
explanation.definitionFit: A bight is a long, gently curving bay in a coastline.

clue.text: It's more conspicuous, say, in Little Rock?

indicators.note: say signals that the word for more conspicuous is spoken, giving a word of the same sound

parts.note: bolder means more striking or prominent

explanation.surface: Something stands out more in an Arkansas city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little Rock' looks like the Arkansas city, but only 'Rock' defines; the question mark admits a big stone is hardly little.
explanation.definitionFit: A boulder is a large stone worn smooth by weather or water.

clue.text: American thug pinches a doctor's decoration

indicators.note: pinches means grips between its ends, so the thug's word holds the other letters

parts.note: goon is American slang for a hired heavy
DR is the abbreviation for doctor

explanation.surface: A US hoodlum steals a physician's medal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pinches' looks like stealing but means gripping: GOON holds A and DR.
explanation.definitionFit: A gadroon is ornamental moulding of reeded or fluted curves on silver or furniture.

clue.text: Announcement from reporter appears to make an impact

explanation.surface: A journalist's statement seems to strike home.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense reads the answer as I'M PRESS, what a reporter might say on arrival.
explanation.definitionFit: To impress is to leave a strong mark on someone; a journalist could introduce themselves as 'I'm press'.

clue.text: Maker of rope — one carried by girl climber

indicators.note: climber in a down entry means the letters go upwards, read from bottom to top
carried by says the girl's word holds the numeral inside it

parts.note: lass is a girl, especially in northern England and Scotland
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A rope supplier: a girl mountaineer carries one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carried by' puts I in LASS; 'climber' then reads LASIS upwards in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Sisal is a plant fibre from agave leaves, used to make cord and twine.

clue.text: In pieces, like articles assembled overseas

parts.note: as means like, as in 'as good as new'
un is a French indefinite article, 'a'
der is a German definite article, 'the'

explanation.surface: Broken up, like goods put together abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overseas' says the articles are foreign: French UN and German DER.
explanation.definitionFit: Asunder means apart or into separate bits, as in 'torn asunder'.

clue.text: Edible treats for screen heroes

explanation.surface: Sweets for the stars of the film.
explanation.definitionFit: Goodies are tasty things to eat, and also the good guys in a film, opposite the baddies.

clue.text: At home for part of main do —- or subsidiary

indicators.note: part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Staying in for some of the big party or a lesser one.
explanation.definitionFit: Being indoors means inside the house rather than out.

clue.text: When Yellow-Dog Dingo benefited Old Man Kangaroo — eventually

definitions.text: When Yellow-Dog Dingo benefited Old Man Kangaroo

explanation.surface: A nod to Kipling's Just So Stories, where a dingo's chase changes a kangaroo.
explanation.walkthrough: In Kipling's 'The Sing-Song of Old Man Kangaroo', the dingo chases the kangaroo all day, and the long chase gives it its powerful legs.
explanation.definitionFit: Eventually means after a long time, ultimately; for the kangaroo, the benefit came from a long chase.
